rows.selection_reason: With no completed experiments, there is zero evidence to guide exploitation, so the priority is establishing a clean, interpretable baseline. config_006 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50, no aggregation, no fusion) is the simplest and most standard single-modality configuration: it uses the most widely adopted image encoder (ResNet-50), the least complex profile setting, and introduces no confounding aggregation or fusion steps. This gives a clear reference performance for the image modality alone. All subsequent experiments—adding RNA (multimodal), switching to multiprofile, changing the image encoder, or testing fusion strategies—can be directly compared against this anchor. Choosing a more complex multimodal or multiprofile configuration first would conflate multiple design decisions and make it impossible to attribute performance to any single choice, wasting the limited budget.

We have only one completed experiment (config_006: image_only, singleprofile, resnet50 → acc 0.208, F1 0.172), which is barely above chance, giving us very sparse evidence. The most critical uncertainty is whether the image modality has meaningful signal at all or whether ResNet50 is simply too weak a representation. Config_045 (image_only, singleprofile, imagenet_vit_l) is a clean single-variable comparison to config_006—only the image encoder changes—so it isolates the effect of representation quality. If ViT-L substantially improves accuracy, it tells us representation is a bottleneck and motivates investing in stronger encoders and multimodal fusion. If it does not, it strongly suggests the image modality has limited discriminative signal, redirecting the search toward RNA-only or multimodal configurations. This is the highest-information-per-experiment choice under the limited budget because it directly addresses the viability of the image modality before committing to more complex multimodal designs.

We have only two completed experiments, both image_only/singleprofile: ResNet50 (acc≈0.208) and ViT-L (acc≈0.227). The core hypothesis of this multimodal cellular profiling study is whether adding RNA information improves on image-only predictions. config_031 (multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, concat) is the cleanest test of this hypothesis because it holds the image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) and profile setting (singleprofile) identical to our best baseline (config_045), changing only the addition of an RNA branch (scvi_n200) with the simplest fusion (concat). This isolates the marginal contribution of RNA. If accuracy improves meaningfully over 0.227, RNA adds signal; if it stays flat or drops, RNA is not helpful under this setup and we should focus budget on image-side improvements (e.g., multiprofile aggregation). Choosing scvi_n200 over scgpt or PCA avoids introducing an additional untested variable, and concat is the most interpretable fusion baseline. This is the highest-information single experiment available given the sparse evidence.

Evidence: config_031 (multimodal, scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, concat) achieved 0.532 accuracy, a massive jump over both image-only baselines (~0.21–0.23). However, we have no RNA-only result, so it is unclear whether the RNA encoder alone accounts for most of this gain or whether the image modality contributes meaningfully. Question: config_024 (rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200) is a direct ablation of the image modality from config_031, holding the RNA encoder and profile setting identical. It isolates the marginal contribution of the image branch. Why best next: Resolving whether images add real value is the single most consequential design question for the remaining budget. If RNA alone matches ~0.53, subsequent effort should focus on RNA encoder/aggregation choices; if it falls well below, images are essential and we should prioritize fusion strategy and image encoder comparisons. No other single experiment reduces this core uncertainty as cleanly.

Evidence: config_031 (multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, concat) achieved 0.532 acc / 0.517 F1, while config_024 (rna_only, scvi_n200, singleprofile) achieved 0.520 acc / 0.498 F1. The multimodal gain over RNA-only is small (+0.012 acc), and we have only tested one RNA encoder (scvi_n200). Uncertainty: We do not yet know whether the RNA encoder choice (scvi_n200 vs. scgpt) materially affects performance, which is a fundamental representation decision that will influence all future multimodal experiments. Question tested: config_037 (multimodal, singleprofile, scgpt + imagenet_vit_l, concat) is a clean single-variable comparison to config_031, isolating the effect of RNA encoder while holding image encoder, profile setting, and fusion constant. Why best next experiment: Under a limited budget, understanding whether RNA representation quality is a key lever (vs. fusion strategy or profile setting) is the highest-information question. If scgpt significantly outperforms or underperforms scvi_n200, it reshapes the search direction for all subsequent multimodal experiments. If they are similar, we can deprioritize RNA encoder and focus on fusion or multiprofile next.

Evidence: The best result so far is config_031 (multimodal, scvi_n200 + VIT_L, concat) at 0.532 acc, but it only marginally exceeds RNA-only scvi_n200 (config_024, 0.520 acc), suggesting the image contribution is small and the fusion strategy may be a bottleneck. All multimodal results used concat fusion; weighted fusion is untested. Question: config_017 changes only the fusion from concat to weighted while keeping the exact same encoders (scvi_n200 + VIT_L) and singleprofile setting as config_031, giving a clean A/B comparison that isolates the effect of fusion strategy. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) It directly extends the top-performing configuration with a single-variable change, maximizing information per experiment. (2) If weighted fusion improves meaningfully over concat, it reveals a lever for further optimization and justifies exploring weighted fusion in multiprofile settings. (3) If it does not improve, it indicates the current encoder pair is near its ceiling with simple fusion, redirecting effort toward multiprofile aggregation or alternative RNA encoders. (4) Under a limited budget, this minimal-change comparison is more informative than jumping to a multiprofile or new-encoder configuration that would confound multiple variables.

Evidence: All 6 completed experiments are singleprofile. The best result is config_017 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, weighted fusion, acc 0.537), with RNA as the dominant signal (rna_only 0.520 vs image_only ~0.22). The untested multiprofile dimension is the largest source of remaining uncertainty. Question: Does aggregating multiple profiles (via avgpool) improve on the best singleprofile result while keeping the same encoders and fusion? Why this experiment: config_005 is the minimal, direct extension of config_017 into the multiprofile setting—same RNA encoder (scvi_n200), same image encoder (imagenet_vit_l), same fusion (weighted)—with only the addition of multiprofile + avgpool aggregation. This isolates the multiprofile effect cleanly. If it beats 0.537, multiprofile is a productive direction and we can then explore transformer aggregation; if it does not, we avoid wasting budget on more complex multiprofile variants. It is the highest-information single experiment under the limited budget.

The strongest finding so far is config_005 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) at 0.706 acc, a large jump over the best singleprofile multimodal (0.537). This single data point shows multiprofile + avgpool is highly effective, but we have no evidence on whether the aggregation method is a bottleneck or whether a more expressive transformer aggregation could push performance further. Config_032 changes exactly one variable from config_005 (aggregation: avgpool → transformer) while holding all else fixed (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, weighted fusion, multiprofile). This cleanly isolates the aggregation effect in the regime where it matters most. If transformer outperforms avgpool, we identify a new optimization axis; if not, we confirm avgpool suffices and can redirect budget to other variables (e.g., RNA encoder or fusion). Under the limited budget, this is the highest-value single-variable extension of our best result.

Evidence: The largest performance jump in the study is from single-profile to multi-profile in the multimodal setting (0.53→0.725), while RNA-only single-profile (scvi_n200) achieves 0.52 and image-only is negligible (~0.21). We have not yet tested whether the multi-profile + transformer aggregation gain is specific to the multimodal interaction or is a general property of aggregating multiple RNA profiles. Question: config_007 (RNA-only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, transformer) directly tests whether multi-profile aggregation alone, without any image modality, can reproduce the large accuracy gain. Why this is the best next experiment: If RNA-only multi-profile also jumps toward ~0.70, the gain is driven by RNA profile aggregation and the image contributes less than assumed, redirecting effort toward better RNA aggregation. If it stays near 0.52, the multi-profile gain is specifically a multimodal interaction effect, confirming that image+RNA synergy is essential and justifying continued investment in multimodal multi-profile configurations. This single experiment resolves a high-uncertainty mechanistic question that would significantly reshape the remaining search strategy, making it more informative than a small incremental fusion-type or encoder swap on the already-strong multimodal multi-profile setting.

The current best configuration is config_032 (scvi_n200, vit_l, transformer, weighted) at 0.725 acc. In single-profile multimodal, weighted vs concat fusion showed a negligible difference (0.537 vs 0.532, config_017 vs config_031), but we have not tested this in the multiprofile+transformer regime where aggregation is more complex. Config_029 (scvi_n200, vit_l, transformer, concat) is a clean single-variable comparison to config_032, isolating the fusion strategy's effect when transformer aggregation is active. If concat performs comparably, it simplifies the design space and confirms fusion type is a low-priority decision; if it underperforms meaningfully, it validates that weighted fusion is specifically important in the multiprofile setting. Under a limited budget, this experiment reduces uncertainty about an important design axis (fusion) at the current performance frontier without changing multiple variables simultaneously.
